obligation: Process personal data only for a lawful purpose, and only on (a) consent or (b) a s.7 legitimate use. Every processing activity needs a recorded lawful ground.

Every consent request is accompanied or preceded by a notice. The notice states the personal data and purpose, how to withdraw consent and exercise s.13 grievance rights, and how to complain to the Board.
For consent given before commencement, send a notice with the same contents "as soon as reasonably practicable". Processing may continue until withdrawal.
Offer the notice in English or any of the 22 Eighth Schedule languages.
Consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action (no pre-ticked boxes), and limited to data necessary for the specified purpose.
Any part of a consent that infringes the Act or other law (e.g. waiving the right to complain) is invalid to that extent. Templates must not contain such clauses.
The consent request is in clear, plain language, can be read in English or any Eighth Schedule language, and shows the contact details of the DPO or authorised person.
Consent can be withdrawn at any time, as easily as it was given.
On withdrawal, stop processing within a reasonable time and make Data Processors stop, unless law requires or authorises processing. Earlier processing stays lawful.
The principal may give, manage, review or withdraw consent through a Consent Manager, who is accountable to her.
Consent Managers must be registered with the Board. The DF should accept artefacts only from registered CMs.
Where consent is the basis, the DF must prove that notice was given and consent obtained in accordance with law. This needs a tamper-evident record.
Legitimate use: data voluntarily provided for a specified purpose where the principal has not objected. Processing stops when she says she no longer wants it.

The State or its instrumentalities may process data to provide a subsidy, benefit, service, certificate, licence or permit. This applies where (i) the principal previously consented to any such benefit, or (ii) the data sits in a notified State database or register. Processing follows the Second Schedule standards (see CMP-052, CMP-053).
Legitimate use: the State performing a function under law, or for sovereignty and integrity or security of the State.
Legitimate use: fulfilling a legal obligation to disclose information to the State, in line with that law's disclosure provisions.
Legitimate use: complying with a judgment, decree or order (Indian), or a foreign judgment on contractual/civil claims.

Legitimate uses: medical emergency threatening life or health (f); treatment or health services during an epidemic or outbreak (g); safety and assistance during a disaster (DM Act s.2(d)) or breakdown of public order (h).

Legitimate use: employment purposes, safeguarding the employer (espionage, trade secrets, classified information), and services or benefits sought by an employee. This covers government staff workflows (HRMS, leave, APAR).
The DF stays responsible for processing by its Data Processors, and may engage a processor only under a valid contract. This covers the cloud/SDC/NIC host and the system integrator.
If data is used for a decision affecting the principal, or disclosed to another DF, ensure it is complete, accurate and consistent.
Put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures to make the Act effective.
Protect personal data, including at processors, with reasonable security safeguards to prevent breach. Penalty up to Rs 250 crore (Schedule item 1).
On a personal data breach, intimate the Board and each affected principal (form per Rule 7). Penalty up to Rs 200 crore (item 2).
Erase data when consent is withdrawn or when the purpose is no longer served, whichever is earlier, unless law requires retention. Make processors erase too. Disapplied for the State by s.17(4).

The purpose is deemed no longer served if the principal does not approach the DF or exercise rights for the prescribed period. "Approach" means she initiated contact in person, electronically or physically.
Publish the business contact information of the DPO (if applicable) or a person who can answer processing questions.
Set up an effective grievance redressal mechanism.

Obtain the verifiable consent of a parent before processing a child's (<18) data. Obtain the lawful guardian's consent before processing data of a person with disability who has a lawful guardian. Penalty for s.9 breach up to Rs 200 crore.
Do not process a child's data in a way likely to harm the child's well-being.
No tracking, behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising directed at children (subject to Fourth Schedule exemptions).
If notified as SDF, appoint a DPO who represents the SDF, is based in India, answers to the Board of Directors or equivalent governing body, and is the grievance contact point.
If SDF, appoint an independent data auditor to evaluate compliance.

citation: s.10(2)(c) (as amended by S.O. 5458(E): "periodic data audit")
obligation: If SDF, carry out a periodic DPIA (rights, purposes, risk assessment and management), a periodic data audit and other prescribed measures. Penalty up to Rs 150 crore.

On request, give the principal (i) a summary of her data being processed and the processing activities, and (ii) the identities of all DFs and processors it was shared with, plus a description of the data shared.
Sharing with an authorised DF on written request, for offence or cyber-incident prevention, investigation or prosecution, need not be disclosed in the access response.

On request, correct inaccurate or misleading data, complete incomplete data and update data. For the State, s.12(2) does not apply where processing involves no decision affecting the principal (s.17(4)).
On an erasure request, erase unless retention is needed for the specified purpose or by law. Disapplied for the State by s.17(4).
Provide readily available grievance redressal, and respond within the prescribed period (Rule 14(3): at most 90 days). The principal must exhaust this before approaching the Board.
The principal may nominate another individual to exercise her rights on death or incapacity (unsoundness of mind or infirmity of body).

Duties of principals: no impersonation, no suppression of material information for State-issued IDs, no false or frivolous grievances, only verifiably authentic information for correction/erasure. Penalty up to Rs 10,000.
Cross-border transfer is allowed except to countries the Centre notifies (negative list). Stricter sectoral laws prevail.

Exemptions. (1) Chapter II except ss.8(1) and 8(5), Chapter III and s.16 do not apply to: legal claims; courts and quasi-judicial or regulatory bodies; offence prevention and investigation; foreign principals under contract; schemes of arrangement; and loan-default asset tracing. (2)(a) The whole Act does not apply to State instrumentalities the Centre notifies (sovereignty, security, public order etc.). (2)(b) Research, archiving and statistics meeting the Second Schedule standards and not used for individual decisions. (3) Notified DFs and startups are exempt from s.5, 8(3), 8(7), 10, 11. (4) For the State: no s.8(7), no s.12(3), and no s.12(2) when no decision is made. (5) Time-bound notified exemptions within 5 years of commencement. Security (s.8(5)) still applies to s.17(1) cases.

Penalty caps: s.8(5) security Rs 250 cr; s.8(6) breach notice Rs 200 cr; s.9 children Rs 200 cr; s.10 SDF Rs 150 cr; s.15 principal duties Rs 10,000; voluntary undertaking breach up to the original cap; any other breach Rs 50 cr. These are not software requirements; use them for risk weighting.

IT Act s.43A (body-corporate compensation for negligent SPDI handling) is omitted, along with its rule-making power s.87(2)(ob). The SPDI Rules 2011 lose their parent provision. Until then they apply to body-corporate deployers.
RTI Act s.8(1)(j) now exempts "information which relates to personal information" (the public-interest override was removed). Public information officers can rely on this exemption.
The notice stands alone: it is understandable on its own, not buried in terms and conditions.
The notice gives, in clear and plain language, (i) an itemised description of the personal data and (ii) the specified purpose(s), with a specific description of the goods, services or uses enabled.
The notice gives the particular communication link to the DF's website/app and other means to (i) withdraw consent as easily as it was given, (ii) exercise rights, and (iii) complain to the Board.

Consent Managers register with the Board. Conditions include: an Indian company, net worth of at least Rs 2 crore, and independent certification of the interoperable platform against the Board's standards. Relevant to Sangam only as an integrating DF.

CM obligations: route consent directly or via another DF; data must not be readable by the CM; keep a record of consents given, denied and withdrawn, of notices, and of sharing; give access and a machine-readable export; keep records at least 7 years. The DF side must exchange artefacts and logs in a compatible way.

State processing for s.7(b) benefits (under law, policy or public funds) must meet these standards: lawful; limited to s.7(b) uses; data minimisation; reasonable efforts at completeness, accuracy and consistency; retention only while required or by law; reasonable security safeguards; accountability of the person deciding purpose and means.

When processing under s.7(b), give the principal an intimation containing: business contact of a person who can answer questions; the link to the website/app and other means to exercise rights; and consistency with other applicable Central policy or law.
Secure data through encryption, obfuscation, masking or virtual tokens.
Control access to the computer resources used by the DF and processor.
Provide visibility on access to personal data through logs, monitoring and review, so that unauthorised access can be detected, investigated and remediated.
Provide continuity measures, e.g. data backups, for loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability.
Retain such logs and personal data for one year for detection, investigation and continuity, unless another law requires otherwise.
DF-processor contracts must contain security safeguard clauses.
Adopt appropriate technical and organisational measures to make the safeguards effective.

On becoming aware of a breach, tell each affected principal, without delay and concisely, through her user account or registered communication mode: (a) description (nature, extent, timing); (b) likely consequences for her; (c) mitigation measures taken or in progress; (d) safety measures she can take; (e) business contact of a person who can answer queries.
Tell the Board without delay: description of the breach, including nature, extent, timing, location and likely impact.

Within 72 hours of becoming aware (or a longer period the Board allows on written request), give the Board: (i) updated, detailed description; (ii) broad facts on the events, circumstances and reasons; (iii) mitigation measures implemented or proposed; (iv) findings about the person who caused it; (v) remedial measures to prevent recurrence; (vi) a report on the intimations given to principals.

Erase data after the Third Schedule period if the principal has neither approached nor exercised rights. This applies only to: e-commerce entities with ≥2 crore registered users in India; online gaming intermediaries with ≥50 lakh; social media intermediaries with ≥2 crore. Period: 3 years from the last approach or exercise of rights, or from commencement of the Rules, whichever is latest. It does not cover the user-account access or virtual-token access purposes. Government deployers usually fall outside these classes, and the State is exempt from s.8(7) by s.17(4).
At least 48 hours before erasure under r.8, tell the principal that data will be erased unless she logs in, contacts the DF or exercises rights.

For all processing (by DF or processor), retain the personal data, associated traffic data and processing logs for at least one year from the date of processing, for the Seventh Schedule purposes. Then erase, unless other law or a government notification requires longer. The rule's illustration says this holds even if the account is deleted, and processors must also retain.
Prominently publish on the website/app, and mention in every response to a rights request, the business contact of the DPO (if applicable) or a person who can answer questions.

Before processing a child's data, obtain the parent's verifiable consent. Do due diligence that the parent is an identifiable adult (18+) using reliable identity and age details already held by the DF.

Or use identity/age details voluntarily provided (i) by the individual, or (ii) through a virtual token mapped to those details, issued by an authorised entity (one entrusted by law or government, or its appointee), including details or tokens verified by a Digital Locker service provider.

For a person with disability, do due diligence that the guardian was appointed by (a) a court, (b) a designated authority under RPwD Act 2016 s.15, or (c) a local level committee under the National Trust Act 1999 s.13, under the applicable guardianship law.

s.9(1) and (3) do not apply to: clinical/mental health establishments and healthcare professionals (health services); allied healthcare professionals (treatment plan); educational institutions (tracking/monitoring for educational activities or child safety); crèches/day care (safety); child transport providers (location during travel). Each is limited to what is necessary.

Purpose exemptions from s.9(1) and (3): (1) exercising a power or function in the child's interest under law; (2) s.7(b) subsidy/benefit/certificate/licence for a child; (3) email-only account creation; (4) real-time location for the child's safety; (5) blocking harmful content or ads; (6) confirming the user is not a child / Rule 10 due diligence.
If SDF: once every 12 months from notification, carry out a DPIA and an audit. The assessor must give the Board a report of significant observations.

If SDF: due diligence that technical measures, including algorithmic software, used to host, display, upload, modify, publish, transmit, store, update or share personal data pose no likely risk to principals' rights. This covers Sangam's DMN rules and any AI/ML scoring.
If SDF: personal data specified by the Centre (on a committee's recommendation), and the traffic data of its flow, must not be transferred outside India.
Prominently publish (a) the means to make a rights request and (b) the identifier needed: username, application reference number, enrolment ID, email, mobile, licence number etc.
The principal requests through the published means, giving the required particulars. The system must authenticate the requester against the identifier.
Publish the grievance response period, a reasonable period not exceeding 90 days, and implement technical and organisational measures to meet it.
The principal may nominate one or more individuals, using the DF's means and particulars, under its terms and applicable law.
Transfer abroad is subject to any Central general or special order on making data available to a foreign State or entities it controls.
The Act does not apply to research, archiving or statistical processing done under the Second Schedule standards (lawful, minimised, accurate, retention-limited, secure, accountable).
The Board completes inquiries within 6 months of the intimation or complaint (extendable by 3 months at a time). The DF must be able to produce evidence quickly.
The Board and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) work as digital offices. Appeals are filed digitally with the TRAI-Act fee, payable by UPI. This is a deployer process.

The Centre, through authorised persons, may require a DF or intermediary to furnish information. Purposes: State use for sovereignty and security; State functions or legal disclosures; SDF assessment. It may forbid telling the principal where security is involved.

All service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and Government organisations synchronise all ICT system clocks to the NTP servers of NIC or NPL, or servers traceable to them. Multi-geography entities may use another accurate source that does not deviate from NPL/NIC.
IST is not mandatory; UTC is fine, but record the time zone with the timestamp. NIC servers: samay1.nic.in, samay2.nic.in; NPL: time.nplindia.org. Cloud-native time is allowed if it does not deviate.

Report the Annexure I incident types (20 types; list in §5) to CERT-In within 6 hours of noticing, or of being told about, the incident. Channels: email incident@cert-in.org.in, phone 1800-11-4949, fax 1800-11-6969, using the format on the CERT-In website.
If all the details in the CERT-In incident reporting form are not available within 6 hours, report what is known and add the rest later within reasonable time.
Act on CERT-In orders and directions and give information or assistance in the format (up to near real-time) and timeframe specified. Non-compliance is treated as a breach.
Designate a Point of Contact to interface with CERT-In. Send name, designation, organisation, office address, email, mobile, office phone and fax to info@cert-in.org.in, and keep it updated.
Enable logs of all ICT systems and keep them securely for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction. Provide them with any incident report or on CERT-In's direction.

The FAQ (Q35) says logs may also be stored outside India if they can be produced in reasonable time. Q36 says entities serving Indian users must maintain logs in Indian jurisdiction. For government, keep them in India (see CMP-104, CMP-131). Log types include firewall, IPS, SIEM, web, DB, mail, proxy, application, SSH and VPN. Record both successful and unsuccessful events.
Log requests come from a CERT-In officer not below Deputy Secretary rank. Verify the requester before exporting.

Data centres, VPS, cloud and VPN providers keep subscriber KYC records (validated names, hire period, IPs, registration email/IP/timestamp, purpose, validated address/phone, ownership pattern) for 5 years after cancellation. This does not apply to Sangam as software. It applies to the deployer's hosting provider (MeitY CSP/SDC/NIC). Enterprise VPNs are excluded (FAQ Q34).
Virtual-asset service providers, exchanges and custodian wallets keep KYC and transaction records for 5 years. Not applicable to a government workflow platform.

citation: Directions closing para; IT Act s.70B(7) as amended
obligation: Failing to furnish information or comply may draw s.70B(7) action. The fine was raised from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 1 crore by the Jan Vishwas Act 2023 (in force 30-11-2023).

Unique user IDs; identity provisioning through a workflow with checks; review at least every six months with a report to the head of department; immediate deactivation on exit; RBAC from an access matrix; periodic privilege review.

citation: Gov. Entities Guidelines s.5.3-5.4, Annexure s.5.22-5.23
obligation: MFA as far as possible. Government users log in through a national SSO (e-Pramaan, Parichay/Jan Parichay (NIC) or DigiLocker). Public users get MFA/2FA.
Terminate sessions after 15 minutes of inactivity, with re-authentication. Encrypt passwords in transit. Minimum 8 characters, complex. Change at least every 120 days (where passwords are used).
Segregation of duties; separate admin accounts per role with least privilege.

Secure SDLC; privacy of citizen data at each stage; server-side validation; HTTPS with a valid certificate; safe error handling; VAPT at least yearly or on change, including APIs; continuous log monitoring with alerts; binary integrity checks.

Classify personal data and encrypt it in transit and at rest; DLP; harden DB defaults; breach detection and alerting; documented backup policy (data, DB, keys, configs); fix IDOR, SQL injection and insecure APIs; micro-segmentation for DB access.
Cloud: shared-responsibility review; no public storage exposure; least privilege; cloud-native logging; MFA on accounts.
Host applications only in government data centres or MeitY-empanelled CSPs. Never inside a Ministry/Department LAN segment.
Audit applications through a CERT-In empanelled auditor before hosting, at least annually and after major changes. Host only after security-audit clearance. Share reports with the CISO.

Use NIC DNS (1.10.10.10 / 2409::1) and NIC NTP; review server logs daily; keep logs on a separate server; logging on all ICT systems including applications and DBs; retain logs at least 180 days unless the CISO says otherwise; onboard to NIC PRATIMAAN (SIEM) / IPAM, with State departments via state NIC centres.
Internal security audit at least every 6 months; third-party audit at least yearly; audit before and after major implementation; follow-up audits.
Documented incident handling procedures; incident analysis reports; up-to-date point-of-contact list; active log monitoring by a security team.

citation: Comprehensive Cyber Security Audit Policy Guidelines v1.0
obligation: Comprehensive audit at least annually, scoped to an up-to-date asset inventory, risk-based and evidence-based, using CERT-In templates. Applications handling sensitive personal data use the CERT-In audit checklist (reported as 282 control points). Binding on empanelled auditors and auditees.

SBOM (21 minimum fields reported), CBOM, AIBOM etc. Applicable to public sector and government entities and their software suppliers, especially in procurement. The guidelines are described as voluntary but expected in procurement.

A body corporate that is negligent with SPDI and causes wrongful loss or gain must pay compensation. A government department is not a "body corporate", but PSUs, corporations and system integrators may be. Ends when DPDP s.44(2) commences.

citation: IT Act s.72A (as amended by Jan Vishwas Act)
obligation: Disclosing personal information obtained under a lawful contract, without consent or in breach of contract, with intent to cause wrongful loss or gain, carries a penalty up to Rs 25 lakh (no longer imprisonment, from 30-11-2023). Relevant to Sangam vendors and integrators.
A person given powers under the IT Act who discloses records without consent faces a penalty up to Rs 5 lakh.

Criminal offences for computer-related acts under s.43 (hacking, damage, data theft), and for capturing or publishing images of a private area without consent. Sangam must not facilitate these; access controls and logs support investigation.
Intermediaries must preserve and retain information as the Centre specifies. Non-compliance draws a penalty up to Rs 25 lakh (amended). Applies to the deployer only if it acts as an intermediary.

citation: IT Act s.69, s.69A, s.69B (+ 2009 Rules)
obligation: Lawful interception, monitoring and decryption orders (s.69); blocking orders (s.69A); traffic-data monitoring for cyber security (s.69B; penalty amended to up to 1 year or Rs 1 crore fine). The deployer must be able to comply with lawful orders, keeping orders confidential.

citation: IT Act s.70 + Protected System Rules 2018
obligation: If a Sangam deployment is declared a protected system (CII), the organisation must have a CISO, an ISMS, regular audits, and report incidents to NCIIPC/CERT-In. Access is limited to authorised persons.
CERT-In may call for information and give directions. Failing to comply carries up to 1 year imprisonment or a fine up to Rs 1 crore (amended).

SPDI means: password; financial info (bank, card, payment instrument); physical, physiological and mental health; sexual orientation; medical records; biometrics. Public-domain and RTI-furnished data is excluded. Sangam field classification should tag these.
Publish a privacy policy on the website covering: practices; types of SPDI collected; purpose; disclosure; security practices.

Obtain written (letter, fax, email) consent for the purpose before collecting SPDI. Collect only for a lawful, necessary purpose. Tell the person the fact of collection, purpose, recipients, and the collecting and retaining agency. Retain no longer than needed. Use only for the stated purpose. Offer the option not to provide, and to withdraw in writing.
Let providers review their information and correct inaccurate or deficient data.

Designate a Grievance Officer, publish name and contact on the website, and redress grievances within one month of receipt. Stricter than DPDP's 90 days for SPDI-covered body corporates until 13-05-2027.

Disclosing SPDI to third parties needs prior permission, unless contracted or legally required. Government agencies mandated by law get it on a written request stating the purpose. Never publish SPDI, and recipients must not disclose further.
Transfer SPDI (in India or abroad) only to an entity giving the same level of protection, and only if necessary for the contract or with consent.

Reasonable security practices: a documented information security programme and policies (managerial, technical, operational and physical controls), demonstrable after a breach. IS/ISO/IEC 27001 is deemed compliant if certified or audited by an independent government-approved auditor at least once a year or on significant upgrade.

(g) Preserve removed or disabled content and associated records for 180 days (or longer if a court or agency asks). (h) Keep a user's registration information for 180 days after cancellation or withdrawal of registration.
Secure the computer resource following the SPDI Rules 2011 reasonable security practices.
Provide information or assistance to lawfully authorised agencies no later than 72 hours after receiving an order (identity verification, offences, cyber security incidents).

Publish the Grievance Officer's name and contact and the complaint mechanism. Acknowledge within 24 hours and resolve within 15 days. Removal requests under r.3(1)(b) are resolved within 72 hours. Private-area/impersonation content is removed within 24 hours. Appeal to the Grievance Appellate Committee within 30 days.

citation: MeitY Cloud contractual-terms guidelines (2017); CSP empanelment
obligation: Government data on cloud must reside in India, with a localisation clause in contracts. Use only MeitY-empanelled CSPs that hold a valid STQC audit (annual surveillance audit).

citation: MeghRaj / GI Cloud policy; National Data Centre Policy (draft 2020)
obligation: Use GI Cloud and empanelled data centres for government workloads; prefer government community cloud. Policy direction rather than a statute.
Government websites and apps conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, based on RPwD Act 2016, IT Act and ISO 23026. Applies to citizen-facing Sangam forms, tasklists and notices.
Government sites are expected to be bilingual (English and Hindi) and to offer regional languages. The exact clause wording was not checked.
Publish website policies (privacy, copyright, hyperlinking, terms) and follow the CERT-In-drafted security chapter (HTTPS, security audit before hosting).

citation: RPwD Act 2016 s.40, s.46 and RPwD Rules 2017 r.15
obligation: Service providers and government establishments must make ICT accessible to the prescribed standard (GIGW).

citation: Email Policy of GoI (2014) / Policy on Use of IT Resources (2014)
obligation: Official communication uses the government email service (gov.in / nic.in). Official data is not routed through private email services. Sangam's notification sender must support the NIC SMTP relay and gov.in sender domains.

citation: NISPG (MHA, National Information Security Policy & Guidelines)
obligation: Classify government information (Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, Restricted) and apply handling controls. The document is not public, so obligations cannot be verified.

citation: IT Act s.43A / SPDI r.8 and S8 Annexure 5.21
obligation: All endpoints HTTPS with a valid TLS certificate (no plain HTTP in production).

Core biometric information must never be shared or stored beyond authentication. Identity information is used only for the purpose submitted. The Aadhaar number must not be published, displayed or posted publicly except as regulations allow.
Do not publicly display the Aadhaar number. Do not make public any database or record containing Aadhaar numbers unless they are redacted or masked. Mask by default in all displays (UIDAI guidance).

citation: UIDAI ADV circular 25-07-2017 → Circular No. 8 of 2025 (18-07-2025) + ADV/HSM FAQs (03-11-2025)
obligation: Requesting Entities (AUA/KUA/Sub-AUA) store Aadhaar numbers, UID tokens, e-KYC XML/PDF and Aadhaar-linked demographic data only in an Aadhaar Data Vault. The ADV is encrypted with AES-256 or above, keys are kept in an HSM, and it is hosted on RE premises, a MeitY-empanelled Government Community Cloud, or ADV-as-a-service. Use reference keys in all business systems; strict access control and logging. ADV duties do not apply to non-RE entities (e.g. offline verification or employee records). Data in the ADV must come post-authentication from UIDAI.
Reported to supersede the 2017 circular and Circular 8 of 2025. Contents not read; re-check before encoding.

citation: Aadhaar Act s.41 (as amended by Jan Vishwas Act)
obligation: Contravention by a requesting entity or enrolling agency carries a penalty up to Rs 1 lakh (individual) or Rs 10 lakh (company), from 30-11-2023.
Public records must not be taken or transmitted out of India without prior Central approval (except for official purposes). This supports India-only hosting of workflow records.

citation: PRA s.8 + Rules (retention schedules, appraisal, review, destruction register)
obligation: Public records may be destroyed only under a retention schedule, drawn up with the National Archives for substantive-function records, after review and recording. Destruction must be recorded. Contravening s.4 or s.8 is punishable with up to 5 years and/or a fine up to Rs 10,000. DPDP erasure must give way to records retention (an "any law" exception under s.8(7) and s.12(3)).
Each records creating agency designates a Records Officer responsible for record management and safe custody.

citation: Tamil Nadu Cyber Security Policy 2020 / CSP 2.0 (G.O. 2024)
obligation: All TN State Government IT assets fall under CERT-TN, and departments report to TN-CERT (CERT-In takes the lead in crises). Incidents must therefore go to CERT-TN in addition to CERT-In.

citation: State CERTs generally (e.g. Kerala, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Odisha)
obligation: Several states run state CERTs or SOCs and expect incidents to be shared with them. Specific mandates not verified.

citation: State Data Centre (SDC) hosting under NeGP/state IT policies
obligation: Many states require state applications to be hosted in the State Data Centre or state cloud. Mandates differ by state and were not verified individually.

The authority and agencies keep the Jan-Aadhaar repository data secure and confidential. Identity information, photograph and Jan-Aadhaar ID are not shared or publicly displayed except as the Act or rules allow. Authentication logs are shared with the holder on request. Breach carries a fine up to Rs 10,000. This applies when a Sangam deployment in Rajasthan consumes Jan-Aadhaar data.

citation: Telangana Open Data Policy 2016 / TGDeX; Karnataka Open Data Policy 2021 (data exchange framework under revision)
obligation: Open-data policies call for shareable, non-personal datasets to be published. Karnataka is revising its policy to align with DPDP. Datasets must be de-identified before publication.

citation: State official-language acts (e.g. state Official Language Acts)
obligation: Notices to citizens in the state's official language are often required alongside English or Hindi. DPDP s.5(3) already requires an Eighth Schedule language option.
